GK-05.c01: To control a truck or bus you control its **speed** and its **direction**.
The **4 skills** are accelerating, steering, stopping, and backing safely.
Wear your seatbelt on the road, and set the **parking brake** whenever you leave the vehicle, because an empty parked truck can roll away.
GK-05.c02: Don't roll back: with a manual, let the clutch **partly out** before your right foot leaves the brake.
Release the parking brake **only after** the engine gives enough power to hold the vehicle; a tractor-trailer may also use the trailer hand valve.
Speed up smoothly and gradually, because jerky starts can damage the vehicle and the **coupling**.
On poor traction, speed up very gradually; if the drive wheels spin → **take your foot off the accelerator**.
GK-05.c03: Grip the wheel firmly with **both hands**, on **opposite sides** of the wheel.
Why: hitting a curb or pothole can jerk the wheel out of a loose grip.
GK-05.c04: Press the brake pedal down **gradually**; the pressure needed depends on your speed and how fast you must stop.
With a manual, push in the clutch once the engine has slowed to **near idle**, so the engine keeps running as you stop.
GK-05.c05: Backing is **always dangerous**, so avoid it when you can and park where you can pull forward out.
Follow the **6 rules**: proper start position, get out and look at your path, use both mirrors, back slowly, turn toward the driver's side, use a helper.
Back in the **lowest reverse gear** so you can fix errors and stop quickly.
Back toward the **driver's (left) side**, even if you must drive around the block, because your view on the right (blind) side is poor.
A helper stands near the back **where you can see them**; the most important hand signal to agree on is **"STOP."**
GK-05.c06: Backing a trailer → turn the steering wheel the **opposite** way, then follow the trailer once it begins to turn.
Example: to move the trailer's rear left, turn the wheel **right**, then turn back left to follow it.
Keep the path straight when possible, or curve toward the driver's side, and back **slowly**.
Correct drift immediately by steering **toward the drift**, and use **pull-ups** to reposition whenever needed.
GK-05.c07: If you can't get into the right gear while driving, you have **less control** of the vehicle.
GK-05.c08: Most heavy vehicles with an **unsynchronized** manual require double clutching (clutch in twice per shift); synchronized ones do not.
Double clutching has **5 steps**; in Neutral, let rpm drop before an upshift but press the accelerator to **raise** rpm before a downshift.
Can't get into gear → don't force it: back to Neutral, release the clutch, match engine rpm to road speed, try again.
Know when to shift by **engine speed (rpm)** or **road speed (mph)**; with progressive shifting the shift rpm rises in higher gears.
Downshift **before** starting down a hill, usually to a gear lower than the climbing gear, and **before** entering a curve.
GK-05.c09: Multi-speed rear axles and auxiliary transmissions give the vehicle **extra gears**.
They are usually worked by a **knob or switch** on the main shift lever; shift patterns vary, so learn the vehicle you drive.
GK-05.c10: On a downgrade, select a **low range** to get more engine braking.
A low range keeps the transmission from shifting up past the chosen gear, unless the engine exceeds its **governor rpm**.
GK-05.c11: A retarder helps slow the vehicle, giving **less brake wear** and another way to slow down.
The **4 types** are exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric; the driver can turn any retarder on or off.
When on, it brakes **only the drive wheels**, each time your foot comes fully off the accelerator.
Turn the retarder **OFF** on wet, icy, or snow-covered roads, because it can make the drive wheels skid.
